summary: Walkthrough of Redwood SDKs (Python and TypeScript), auth options, env setup, and quickstarts. Agreed next steps: share sample repo, security docs, and schedule a benchmark PoC. Customer interested in hosted API for initial pilot, evaluating Dedicated/Private for production depending on data residency and latency tests.

Environment variables and local dev setup
Example integration patterns for web frontend + server
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Maya from our solutions engineering team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] David: Good, thanks. David here, CTO at Acme Payments. We have Priya and Marco on the line too.
[00:12] Priya: Hey all.
[00:15] Maya: Hi, quick agenda: we planned an SDK integration walkthrough — Python and TypeScript — cover auth, env setup, quickstarts, then leave time for Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:24] Marco: Yeah perfect. We mainly want to see the pattern for server->Redwood and web frontend streaming.
[00:30] Jordan: Great. Quick background from you David? where you're planning to use the LLM and any constraints?
[00:37] David: We're building an intelligent payments assistant inside the merchant dashboard, so it needs to fetch transaction context and generate short responses. Latency is a concern — target under 300ms tail for short prompts; also data residency and SOC2 compliance are required. We'll try hosted first, but if latency or residency is a blocker we may look at Dedicated or Private.
[00:54] Maya: Makes sense. We'll show hosted SDK flow first — it's the fastest path to prod for a POC — and then call out differences for Dedicated/Private.
[01:02] Jordan: I'll share the quickstart repo after the call.
[01:06] Maya: Alright jumping in: Python SDK. The typical pattern is set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then call the client. Example — pseudo: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — then client.chat.create(...)
[01:25] Marco: Is that the official package name?
[01:27] Maya: In the repo it's redwood-sdk-python; our pypi name may vary, but the quickstart links include exact install commands.
[01:33] Priya: Any differences between API key auth and SSO? We use SSO internally and would prefer short-lived credentials.
[01:40] Maya: For initial POC API keys are easiest. For enterprise you can integrate SAML/SAML2 SSO with short-lived tokens — Redwood supports SSO for the console and mTLS/IdP flows for private deployments; we also support API keys rotated via your KMS. We'll send the SSO and KMS integration docs.
[01:54] David: Cool. How do you recommend storing keys in prod? Our infra uses Vault.
[01:59] Maya: Vault is perfect. Store REDWOOD_API_KEY in Vault and inject into the app as env var at runtime. For Dedicated/Private we can wire KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys.
[02:08] Jordan: Now TypeScript: npm install @redwoodai/sdk or yarn add @redwoodai/sdk (note: package name in repo). Example server code — import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.chat.stream(...).
[02:26] Marco: For streaming to frontend — do we proxy through our server or is there a secure websocket option?
[02:31] Maya: Recommended is server-side proxy. Your backend holds the API key and streams token deltas to the browser over SSE or WebSocket. Direct client-side keys are not recommended. For Private we can do short-lived tokens via the Console and a token-exchange flow if you want to reduce backend work.
[02:49] Priya: Any rate limits on the hosted API? We're worried about bursty traffic during flash sale windows.
[02:55] Jordan: Hosted has tiered quotas and lead time for bursts. Dedicated gives predictable throughput with reserved GPU capacity. For spikes we can configure autoscaling + burst capacity or set up fallback to smaller model variants.
[03:07] David: You mentioned fallback. So if our preferred model is busy it can route to a cheaper variant?
[03:12] Maya: Yes, smart routing — policy-driven. You can set latency or cost policies and automatically fall back to compatible quantized variants. Might be some quality tradeoff but keeps service available.
[03:23] Jordan: Ok I'll show a live quickstart in the browser — switching to the quickstart repo (I pasted link in chat).
[03:30] Maya: I'll share the snippet: Python chat create with messages = [{role: 'system', content: 'You are a payments assistant...'}, {role: 'user', content: user_prompt}] then call client.chat.create and parse the response. Note transcripts may show minor typos in our example.
[03:50] [04:00] Jordan: (screen share) here's the repo structure: /quickstart/python/, /quickstart/ts/, plus a docker-compose for local dev. The python quickstart includes a sample Flask endpoint that proxies to Redwood and exposes SSE to the frontend.
[04:15] Priya: Nice. Does the Flask sample include batching? we might want to batch multiple small prompts to save cost.
[04:21] Maya: There's an example middleware for simple batching and caching — prefix cache and KV cache hints. In hosted we have prefix/KV caching automatically if you enable it, but the client-side can also implement small request coalescing.
[04:34] Marco: Could you clarify KV cache — is that in the runtime or something we need to configure?
[04:39] Maya: KV cache refers to our serving runtime cache for previous prefixes and KV cache for autoregressive caches. It's mostly managed by Redwood; on Dedicated/Private you can tune retention and memory. We'll include a doc snippet.
[04:51] David: On telemetry — does Redwood capture PII in logs by default? We have regulatory constraints.
[04:57] Maya: By default we collect minimal telemetry for performance and billing. For enterprise contracts we can disable retention, or enable redaction. Private deployments keep data in your VPC/on-prem. We'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[05:11] Jordan: I'm dropping the link to the security pack in chat now.
[05:15] [05:30] Priya: For local dev, what's the recommended env setup?
[05:33] Maya: Example .env: REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-..., REDWOOD_API_BASE=https://api.redwood.ai (for hosted), REDWOOD_MODEL=redwood-quant-v1 (example). The TS quickstart also uses NEXT_PUBLIC_RE... only for non-secret client flags. Keep keys server-side.
[05:50] Marco: We use Next.js; any gotchas?
[05:53] Maya: With Next.js put server calls in API routes or app/server components. Use SSE for streaming. Avoid shipping keys to the browser. For SSR it's ok to call the API on the server and hydrate.
[06:06] David: For the PoC we want to test latency on our production-like dataset. How fast can we get a benchmark?
[06:12] Maya: We can run an initial benchmark within a week. For hosted we'll run from our closest region; for Dedicated we'll provision a small reserved pool for more precise numbers. We'll need a representative prompt set and expected concurrency.
[06:24] David: We'll provide prompts and concurrency targets.
[06:27] Maya: Great. Now small demo of streaming in TypeScript — I'll show server->client flow: server calls client.chat.stream and emits token chunks over SSE to browser; client renders as they arrive.
[06:39] [06:45] Jordan: One question that often comes up — SDK versions and pinned dependencies. We recommend pinning the SDK major version and following semver for minor updates. The console shows model compatibility and recommended SDK versions.
[06:58] Priya: Any examples for function calling or structured output? We want to extract JSON for intents.
[07:03] Maya: Yes we support function-calling style with structured outputs. Example in Python we pass a schema and the SDK returns a JSON-safe string; we have helpers to parse and validate. Sometimes the transcripts mis-label function names — the quickstart has a full example.
[07:17] Marco: Does Redwood Optimize help pick quantization levels?
[07:20] Maya: Redwood Optimize analyzes your workload and suggests quantization and batching profiles to hit latency/cost targets. For the PoC we'll run Optimize on your sample prompts to recommend a profile.
[07:33] David: About credentials rotation — do you support short-lived keys via an exchange endpoint?
[07:38] Maya: Yes, we support a token-exchange flow for short-lived tokens; Console can mint tokens scoped to specific models/routes. We'll send the flow doc.
[07:46] [08:00] Jordan: Ok let's go over the quickstart steps so David's team can onboard: 1) Clone repo 2) Install SDK for Python/TS 3) Set REDWOOD_API_KEY in Vault or .env for local dev 4) Run the sample server, see streaming demo 5) Replace sample prompts and run benchmarks 6) Share results with us.
[08:20] Priya: Any sample SLOs or dashboards in Redwood Console? we want to track per-route latency and token cost.
[08:26] Maya: Console has per-route dashboards, tracing hooks, token cost breakdowns and alerts. You'll also get per-token latency percentiles and cold-start metrics. We'll provision a demo org view for you.
[08:40] Marco: Are there SDK examples to instrument tracing? we use OpenTelemetry.
[08:44] Maya: We have integrations for common tracing libs; you can send traces to your collector. We'll include a snippet for OpenTelemetry.
[08:53] David: On pricing — can you share ballpark hosted costs for our expected throughput?
[08:58] Jordan: We'll send a tailored pricing sheet after we get your prompt set and expected concurrency. Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is committed. I'll include both.
[09:08] Priya: One more security Q — does Redwood support VPC peering for Private?
[09:12] Maya: Yes, Private supports VPC peering, and on-prem options for air-gapped deployments. We can also support customer-managed KMS and audit logs.
[09:22] [09:30] Jordan: Cool, we'll recap and then open up to more questions.
[09:33] Marco: Quick nit: sometimes package names in examples are slightly off, we've seen typos in docs before. Can you confirm final package names in the repo?
[09:41] Maya: Good catch — we'll confirm exact package names and versions in the repo before sending.
[09:46] David: Great. On timeline, if we start now can we have a pilot in 2-3 weeks?
[09:52] Maya: Yes, if you provide prompts and test dataset this week we can have a pilot within 2 weeks for hosted tests. Dedicated takes longer due to capacity provisioning.
[10:02] [10:15] Jordan: Alright recap of next steps: Jordan to share SDK quickstart repo + security pack, Maya to run benchmark and initial latency test once sample prompts are provided, David to share prompts and concurrency targets. We'll schedule the benchmark PoC for the week of 2026-08-24.
[10:35] Priya: Sounds good.
[10:37] Marco: Thanks everyone.
[10:40] Maya: Thanks all, I'll follow up in email with links.
[10:44] David: Thanks.
[10:46] Jordan: Bye.
[44:30] (call ended)

Notes: occasional transcription errors in vendor names and package names present in the conversation. Links dropped to chat: quickstart repo, security pack, pricing sheet. The transcript includes high-level code patterns but not full verbatim code blocks.
